opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest with yourself about what actually matters. When time is limited, and it always is, especially if you're running a lab and also trying to build something outside the lab, you can't do everything that's interesting. There are a hundred interesting problems. The real question is which ones are important *and* which ones you're in a uniquely good position to solve.

So my personal rule is to ask: if this problem is solved, does it change what the field can do, or does it just add one more paper to a pile? In embodied intelligence especially, there are a lot of directions where you can get incremental improvements on a benchmark, and that's fine for training students, but it's not where I want to spend my own limited attention. I try to put my own time on the bottlenecks: for robots, things like data, generalization, how you actually get a system to work reliably in the real world rather than in a demo.

The second thing is to think in terms of leverage. A lot of my time goes into choosing directions and setting up the right problems for students, rather than doing every experiment myself. If I pick the right question and the right people are working on it, that's worth much more than me personally grinding on something. So prioritizing research, for me, is partly prioritizing people: who is ready to own a hard problem, and how do I give them the space and resources to do it.

The third thing is being willing to say no, and sometimes to stop. That's actually the hardest part. Researchers get attached to directions. But if you've given something a fair try and the signal isn't there, or the world has moved, for example a foundation model suddenly makes your approach unnecessary, you have to be decisive and cut it. Sunk cost is very expensive when your time is limited.

And finally, I try to keep a connection between research and real-world feedback. Working with actual robots, actual deployments, tells you very quickly which problems are real and which ones only exist on paper. That feedback loop is probably the best prioritization tool I have. It keeps you focused on what truly blocks progress, instead of what's merely fashionable.

r001.rationale: The response favors high-impact bottlenecks over incremental work, but it does not recommend focusing on one or two technologies or clearly say those technologies require breakthroughs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I had to accept is that limited time is not a bug, it's the condition. Everyone at the frontier is time-constrained. So the question isn't how to do everything, it's how to choose what you refuse to do.

My rough framework has three parts.

The first is to be very clear about what the "one question" is. Early on I would chase many interesting threads at once, and I'd end up with five half-finished results and nothing that really moved. Now I force myself to write down, in one sentence, the problem that would matter most if it worked. If I can't write that sentence, I haven't earned the right to spend time on it yet. Most of the prioritization happens there, before any experiment runs.

The second is to separate what only I can do from what anyone can do. There's a lot of research work that looks like research but is really plumbing, data cleaning, reproducing a baseline, writing the tenth version of a figure. That has to get done, but I shouldn't be the one protecting my best hours for it. The hours when my mind is sharpest go to the parts that need judgment: framing the problem, deciding which result is actually surprising, figuring out why something failed. Those are the hours I guard most jealously, and I try to keep them free of meetings.

The third is a willingness to kill things early. Scientists are trained to be persistent, and persistence is real, but most of the time I've lost wasn't on hard problems, it was on problems I had already stopped believing in but kept running out of sunk cost. So I set a checkpoint: by this date, what evidence would make me keep going? If I don't see it, I stop, write a short note on what I learned, and move on. That note is important, because a well-documented failure is still progress and it keeps me from re-exploring the same dead end a year later.

And one more thing I'd add, which is less tactical: when time is short, it's tempting to optimize for output, papers, talks, visible things. I try to optimize instead for understanding, because understanding compounds. A year spent really understanding one phenomenon gives you a kind of intuition that makes the next five problems faster. A year spent producing six incremental results doesn't do that. So in a strange way, having less time has pushed me to be slower and deeper on fewer things, rather than faster on more.

r001.rationale: The response recommends choosing one important research question and going deeper on fewer problems, but it does not recommend focusing on one or two technologies that require breakthroughs.

astra-6.text:
I think you first have to be clear about the question you most want to answer. When time is limited, you can’t pursue every interesting idea, so I would prioritize a problem that matters and where I can make meaningful progress with the resources I have.

Then I’d ask: what is the next experiment or calculation that will reduce the most uncertainty? Sometimes that’s a small test of a key assumption. If the assumption is wrong, finding that out early can save months of work.

I’d also protect some uninterrupted time for thinking. It’s easy to fill your schedule with tasks and still avoid the difficult question. For me, prioritization means choosing what deserves that focused attention—and being willing to set other things aside.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on an important research problem and the next uncertainty-reducing step, but does not recommend concentrating effort on one or two technologies that require breakthroughs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start by asking which question really matters. When time is limited, you can’t pursue every interesting idea, so I would focus on a problem where making progress would change our understanding, and where I have a realistic way to contribute.

Then I’d identify the next step that would reduce the most uncertainty. Sometimes that’s an experiment; sometimes it’s reading carefully or talking with a colleague. The important thing is to avoid confusing being busy with making progress. Protect time for the central question, and be willing to reconsider your priorities when the evidence changes.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on an important research problem, but does not specify one or two technologies or say that they genuinely require breakthroughs.
